title: SIRVALUE: from BASIC to Python
text:
← PreviousSIR model: from BASIC to PythonAll appsNext →Graphing S: from BASIC to Python
This page runs the SIRVALUE program from the BASIC listing below (see page 65), rewritten in Python. The Python runs right here in your browser, and the table shows whatever the program prints. Edit the code and press Run to update it; Reset brings back the original program.
The model is the same as before: susceptible people become infected at a rate of a × S × I, and infected people recover at a rate of b × I, with a = 0.00001 and b = 1 / 14. What’s new is the goal. Instead of printing a value every day, SIRVALUE estimates S, I and R at a single later time, tfinal = 1. It gets there by splitting the interval from tinitial to tfinal into numberofsteps = 10 equal steps, so deltat = (1 - 0) / 10 = 0.1, and taking one Euler step for each.

title: SIRVALUE: from BASIC to Python
text:
Notes from the textbook

Add notes here.






NoteOriginal BASIC program (SIRVALUE.BAS)





 1  DEFDBL A-Z
 2  tinitial = 0
 3  tfinal = 1
 4  t = tinitial
 5  S = 45400
 6  I = 2100
 7  R = 2500
 8  numberofsteps = 10
 9  deltat = (tfinal - tinitial) / numberofsteps
10  FOR k = 1 TO numberofsteps
11          Sprime = -.00001 * S * I
12          Iprime = .00001 * S * I - I / 14
13          Rprime = I / 14
14          deltaS = Sprime * deltat
15          deltaI = Iprime * deltat
16          deltaR = Rprime * deltat
17          t = t + deltat
18          S = S + deltaS
19          I = I + deltaI
20          R = R + deltaR
21  NEXT k
22  PRINT t, S, I, R

title: Graphing S: from BASIC to Python
text:
← PreviousSIRVALUE: from BASIC to PythonAll apps
This page runs a BASIC program that graphs S, the number of susceptible people, over three days. The program is rewritten in Python and runs right here in your browser. Edit the code and press Run to redraw the graph; Reset brings back the original program.
The calculation is the same Euler’s method as in SIRVALUE, now with tfinal = 3 and numberofsteps = 30, so deltat = 0.1. The new part is the drawing. On each pass through the loop, LINE (t, S)-(t + deltat, S + deltaS) draws a straight segment from the current point to the next one, and together the 30 segments form a piecewise-linear approximation to the graph of S. WINDOW (0, 40000)-(3, 45400) sets the coordinates of the screen, so t runs from 0 to 3 across and S runs from 40,000 to 45,400 up. (SCREEN 12 just switches the computer into graphics mode.)
In the Python, window(...) and line(...) do the same jobs as WINDOW and LINE. Try setting numberofsteps to 3 to see the individual segments, or to 300 for a smoother curve.

 8  I = 2100

12  FOR k = 1 TO numberofsteps
13          Sprime = -.00001 * S * I
14          Iprime = .00001 * S * I - I / 14
15          Rprime = I / 14
16          deltaS = Sprime * deltat
17          deltaI = Iprime * deltat
18          deltaR = Rprime * deltat
19          LINE (t, S)-(t + deltat, S + deltaS)
20          t = t + deltat
21          S = S + deltaS
22          I = I + deltaI
23          R = R + deltaR
24  NEXT k

text:

This page runs the SIR (susceptible, infected, recovered) program from the BASIC listing below, rewritten in Python. The Python runs right here in your browser, and the table and graph show whatever the program prints. Edit the code and press Run to update them; Reset brings back the original program.
The model: each day, susceptible people become infected at a rate of a × S × I, and infected people recover at a rate of b × I. In the program, a = 0.00001 is the transmission coefficient and b = 1 / 14 is the recovery coefficient (an illness lasting about two weeks). The program uses Euler’s method: it computes the rates, multiplies by the time step deltat, and adds the changes to S, I and R.
